923.quote_or_event: “Show how base it is to pour down more liquor than one can carry, and not to know the capacity of one's own stomach; show how often the drunkard does things which make him blush when he is sober; state that drunkenness is nothing but a condition of insanity purposely assumed.”
923.explanation: Seneca sets aside Zeno's clever syllogisms against drink and says the honest case against drunkenness is simply to show how shameful it is. He adds that it strips away the sense of shame that otherwise holds men back from wrong.
923.tie_back: Like the Kural, Seneca makes the drunkard's shame, seen through the eyes of others and of his own sober self, the main charge against drink.
923.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 83.18-19 (tr. Richard Mott Gummere)
923._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Wikisource (Gummere, Letter 83 'On Drunkenness', §18; a footnote marker removed). Strong thematic match on the disgrace of drunkenness, but Seneca does not use the Kural's contrast between the forgiving mother and the stricter wise.

951.quote_or_event: “… they seem to have power to encourage and stimulate the generous-minded among our youth, and to make a character which is gently born, and a true lover of what is noble, ready to be possessed by virtue, they are not able to encourage the many to nobility and goodness. For these do not by nature obey the sense of shame, but only fear …”
951.explanation: Aristotle says that moral arguments work only on a character that is already well-born and loves what is noble. The many, by nature, respond to fear of punishment rather than to a sense of shame.
951.tie_back: Like the Kural, Aristotle treats a natural responsiveness to shame as the mark of the well-born, something the many lack.
951.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics X.9, 1179b (tr. W. D. Ross)
951._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on the MIT Internet Classics Archive (Ross, Book X ch. 9). Strong match: shame as an inborn trait of the 'gently born' character. Aristotle's 'gently born' is about natural character more than family lineage, and he does not pair shame with rectitude as the Kural does.

952.quote_or_event: “For the man who loves truth, and is truthful where nothing is at stake, will still more be truthful where something is at stake; he will avoid falsehood as something base, seeing that he avoided it even for its own sake; and such a man is worthy of praise.”
952.explanation: Describing the truthful man as one who is true 'both in life and in word', Aristotle says his honesty is so fixed in his character that he shuns falsehood as shameful even when nothing depends on it.
952.tie_back: Like the Kural's well-born, who never slip from truth, Aristotle's truthful man is steady in truth because lying is base to him.
952.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.7, 1127b (tr. W. D. Ross)
952._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on the MIT Internet Classics Archive (Ross, Book IV ch. 7). Partial match: it covers truthfulness and the sense that falsehood is base, but not the Kural's triad of conduct, truth and shame, nor its link to good birth.

953.quote_or_event: “How much better is it to join kind words to kind actions, and to enhance the value of our gifts by a civil and gracious commendation of them!”
953.explanation: In this part of On Benefits, Seneca says the ready giver 'gives cheerfully and shows his disposition in his countenance' (II.2). He urges joining kind words to the gift (II.3) and warns that harsh words and a contemptuous manner make even kindnesses odious (II.4).
953.tie_back: Seneca's good giver shows the Kural's four marks together: a cheerful face, generosity, kind words and no contempt for the one who receives.
953.source: Seneca, On Benefits (De Beneficiis) II.3, with II.2 and II.4 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
953._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Project Gutenberg (Stewart, eBook #3794, Book II chs. II-IV). Strong match on all four marks. Seneca, however, is describing how to give a benefit well, not the marks of a noble family.

983.quote_or_event: “The foundation of justice, moreover, is good faith; — that is, truth and fidelity to promises and agreements.”
983.explanation: Cicero names the two bonds that hold human society together: justice, and its close kin charity, 'which may also be called kindness or generosity' (I.20). He then rests justice itself on good faith, meaning truth and keeping one's word (I.23).
983.tie_back: Like the Kural, Cicero rests good character on a few named supports, among them generosity, kindness and truth.
983.source: Cicero, De Officiis I.20-23 (tr. Walter Miller)
983._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on LacusCurtius (Miller, Loeb 1913, I.23; I.20 phrase also checked). Partial match: generosity, kindness and truth overlap with the Kural's five pillars, but Cicero gives no list of five and does not include love or shame here.

986.quote_or_event: “it is grievous, when a candidate for public offices, to be defeated by one's inferiors; therefore let him be defeated by Vatinius … That all men may know that these things, which I have deemed Cato worthy to undergo, are not real evils.”
986.explanation: Seneca has Nature explain why she put Cato through every hardship, including losing an election to the inferior Vatinius: to show that such defeats are no true evil to a good man.
986.tie_back: Cato's calm acceptance of defeat by a lesser man is just the touchstone of perfection the Kural names.
986.source: Seneca, Of Providence (De Providentia) 3.14 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
986._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Wikisource (Stewart, Of Providence). The Wikisource text has no section numbers; 3.14 is the standard Latin reference (a deterioribus … Vatinio postferatur). Strong match on accepting defeat by inferiors, though Seneca presents it as a trial set by Nature rather than as a test of one's own humility.

1012.quote_or_event: “Life seems to be common even to plants, but we are seeking what is peculiar to man. Let us exclude, therefore, the life of nutrition and growth. Next there would be a life of perception, but it also seems to be common even to the horse, the ox, and every animal.”
1012.explanation: In his function argument, Aristotle sets aside the life of nourishment and of sensation, which humans share with plants and animals. He looks for what is proper to man alone and finds it in rational, virtuous activity.
1012.tie_back: The argument has the Kural's shape, setting aside the needs shared by all living things to find what marks out the good human. Valluvar finds that mark in shame where Aristotle finds it in reason.
1012.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics I.7, 1097b-1098a (tr. W. D. Ross)
1012._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on the MIT Internet Classics Archive (Ross, Book I ch. 7). Partial match: the structure is very close, but the distinguishing quality differs. Aristotle names rational activity rather than shame, and elsewhere (IV.9) says shame is not a virtue.

1019.quote_or_event: “And does not the legislator and every one who is good for anything, hold this fear in the greatest honour? This is what he terms reverence, and the confidence which is the reverse of this he terms insolence; and the latter he always deems to be a very great evil both to individuals and to states.”
1019.explanation: The Athenian Stranger defines shame as the fear of being thought evil for a dishonourable word or deed. Its opposite, a shameless boldness, he calls a very great evil for persons and cities alike.
1019.tie_back: Plato, like the Kural, treats the loss of shame as a ruin that goes deeper than any single lapse.
1019._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on the MIT Internet Classics Archive (Jowett, Laws Book I). Strong match on shamelessness as a grave evil; Plato does not draw the Kural's contrast between harm to the family's name and harm to all one's goods.

1025.quote_or_event: “For nothing inspires love, nothing conciliates affection, like virtue. Why, in a certain sense we may be said to feel affection even for men we have never seen, owing to their honesty and virtue.”
1025.explanation: Laelius argues that friendship springs from the natural pull of virtue: goodness draws affection so strongly that we love even good men we have never met.
1025.tie_back: This matches the Kural's promise that people gather around the blameless man and treat him as their own kin.
1025.source: Cicero, Laelius de Amicitia, ch. 8 (§§27-28) (tr. E. S. Shuckburgh)
1025._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Project Gutenberg (Shuckburgh, eBook #2808, chapter 8). Strong-to-partial match: virtue wins the affection of others, but Cicero does not speak of a householder who raises his family without wrong.

1026.quote_or_event: “Thus it is clear that household management attends more to men than to the acquisition of inanimate things, and to human excellence more than to the excellence of property which we call wealth, and to the virtue of freemen more than to the virtue of slaves.”
1026.explanation: After describing the head of the household as ruling his children like a king, by love and seniority (I.12), Aristotle concludes that running a household is chiefly about the excellence of its people, not about wealth.
1026.tie_back: Like the Kural, Aristotle treats leading and caring for one's household as a test of a man's character.
1026._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on the MIT Internet Classics Archive (Jowett, Politics Book I, Part XIII). Next-best match: Aristotle analyses household rule rather than calling it the proof of manliness, and his account rests on hierarchies (over women and slaves) that the Kural does not share.

1027.quote_or_event: “Because in the army the most hazardous services are assigned to the bravest soldiers: a general sends his choicest troops to attack the enemy in a midnight ambuscade, to reconnoitre his line of march, or to drive the hostile garrisons from their strong places.”
1027.explanation: Seneca explains why God sends hardship to the best of men: as a general gives the hardest tasks to his finest troops, they say not 'he has dealt hardly with me' but 'he has judged well of me'.
1027.tie_back: Seneca uses the Kural's own battlefield image: the heaviest load falls on those strong enough to bear it.
1027.source: Seneca, Of Providence (De Providentia) 4.8 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
1027._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Wikisource (Stewart, Of Providence). The Wikisource text has no section numbers, so 4.8 follows the standard Latin numbering. Strong match on the battlefield image of burdens falling on the brave; Seneca applies it to divine providence, not to family duty.

1029.quote_or_event: “It is true of the good man too that he does many acts for the sake of his friends and his country, and if necessary dies for them; for he will throw away both wealth and honours and in general the goods that are objects of competition, gaining for himself nobility …”
1029.explanation: Aristotle argues that the good man's sacrifices for others, even his life, are not losses, because he wins for himself the greater good of nobility.
1029.tie_back: This gives the answer the Kural's question implies: the protector's suffering body is not a mere vessel of pain, since his sacrifice is what makes him noble.
1029.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IX.8, 1169a (tr. W. D. Ross)
1029._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on the MIT Internet Classics Archive (Ross, Book IX ch. 8). Partial match: self-sacrifice for others as nobility; Aristotle speaks of friends and country rather than family, and of losing goods rather than bodily suffering.

1030.quote_or_event: “Or how can prosperity be guarded and preserved without friends? The greater it is, the more exposed is it to risk. And in poverty and in other misfortunes men think friends are the only refuge.”
1030.explanation: Opening his account of friendship, Aristotle says that without others to stand by it no fortune can be kept safe, and that in misfortune they are the only support.
1030.tie_back: Like the Kural's family with no one to prop it up, Aristotle's prosperity left without friends is exposed to fall when misfortune strikes.
1030.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VIII.1, 1155a (tr. W. D. Ross)
1030._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on the MIT Internet Classics Archive (Ross, Book VIII ch. 1). Next-best match: the idea of needing a supporter in misfortune is shared, but Aristotle speaks of friends and an individual's prosperity, not of a good man holding up a family, and he has no tree image.
